purpose: Author-created development stress probes, used to choose feedback changes; not a pristine holdout, independent benchmark or real learner data. Groups are author judgements, not clinical labels.

probes.text: Sensitivity measures detected cases rather than the probability of disease among positives.
Sensitivity starts with people who have the condition, whereas predictive value starts with positive results.
A positive result is not conclusive proof of disease.
Prevalence is not irrelevant: it determines how many non-cases can become false positives.
False alarms do not make every screening program useless; benefits and harms need evidence.
Nine true cases among 58.5 positives is about fifteen percent, not ninety percent.
Specificity counts negative results among people without the condition, not true cases among positives.
It is wrong to say that every positive result is a guaranteed diagnosis.
Prevalence matters, but ninety percent sensitivity still means ninety percent of positives are true.
False positives can outnumber true positives when the condition is rare, so the test is completely useless.
The result depends on the starting population, although a positive proves the disease for sure.
False negatives can occur, but a negative result guarantees no condition.
I know sensitivity and predictive value have different denominators, yet both are always the same percentage.
We count all positive results in the denominator; in this case 9 divided by 58.5 is ninety percent.
Sensitivity is ninety percent.
The test is pretty accurate.
There are false positives.
What does prevalence mean?
My friend says a positive result proves disease. Is that really correct?
I am unsure whether the denominator is cases or positives.
All positives are actual cases, without exception.
Prevalence can be ignored for any test.
The true-positive rate is exactly the probability that a positive is a case.
One false alarm makes every screening test pointless.
